police-offences.text: Data coverage for police-reported data varies slightly each year. Cybercrime data for 2025 covers 99.6% of the Canadian population. Coverage for each province/territory is virtually 100% with the exception of New Brunswick (90.9%) due to the exclusion of Saint John Police Force. These percentages are based on police-reported data and populations for the 2025 data cycle.

A criminal incident may be comprised of multiple violations of the law. For the analysis of cyber-related violations, one distinct violation within the incident was identified as the 'cybercrime violation'. The cybercrime violation represents the specific criminal violation within an incident in which a computer or the internet was the target of the crime, or the instrument used to commit the crime. For the majority of incidents, the cybercrime violation and the most serious violation were the same.
Excluded from this table are the small number of police services that do not report to the Uniform Crime Reporting Survey (UCR) 2.

On March 9, 2015, Bill C-13, Protecting Canadians from Online Crime Act, came into effect. As a result of this, a new offence was added to the Criminal Code: non-consensual distribution of intimate images. It also clarified that Criminal Code offences of harassing / indecent communications can be committed by any means of communication. Police services are able to utilize these amendments as their Records Management Systems have been updated as a result.

Historically, police services reported all child pornography offences under a single combined violation code, of which the majority of the offences were possessing child pornography. In early 2016, the Uniform Crime Reporting Survey (UCR) was modified to allow police to report making and distributing child pornography separately from other child pornography offences (for example, possession and accessing child pornography). These data should therefore be interpreted with caution.
Other violations" consists of non-Criminal code offences
The category Luring a child via a computer" also includes the UCR code 1371 "Agreement or Arrangement- sexual offences against a child"."
Calgary Police Service cybercrime data for 2017 and onward are suspected cybercrimes only and should be interpreted with caution.

Hate crime, organized crime and cybercrime data from the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey are now revised back one year with each annual release. This approach was introduced for the 2019 data release and was applied to the 2018 revised data.

Under the authority of the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal (CFPM), the Canadian Forces Military Police Group (CF MP Gp) is now reporting incidents to the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey. They have provided incidents going back to January 2020 and are not included in 2025.

Saint John Police Force cybercrime data are unverified for the years they are included (from 2020 to 2022) and therefore represent incidents that are suspected cybercrimes only and should be interpreted with caution.

Data are based on police-reported incidents that are recorded in police services’ records management systems. Public safety initiatives, levels of public awareness, and changes in policies and technologies available to social media companies may influence the number of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (CSAEM) incidents reported to and recorded by police. As awareness and reporting practices evolve, police services may record fluctuations in both recent and historical incidents, which can affect annual reporting for these criminal violations. Additionally, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police National Child Exploitation Crime Centre (NCECC) serves as the primary point of contact in Canada for investigations related to sexual exploitation of children on the Internet. The NCECC and specialized provincial Internet child exploitation policing units also work in partnership with local police services and jurisdictions. Within this partnership, cases may be forwarded to local police services for processing and investigation. As a result of this exchange, there may be delays in reporting current or historical incidents of CSAEM. This means that the year in which incidents are reported may not correspond to the year in which they occurred. It is important to note that variations between years may reflect differences in the recognition, reporting, and investigation of CSAEM incidents, and not necessarily lower or higher rates of occurrence. Additionally, police resources, policies and the investigational complexities of CSAEM in particular, and child sexual exploitation more generally, can have a considerable impact on police-reported metrics. Due to a substantial increase in the volume and complexity of CSAEM investigations (many of which involve Generative Artificial Intelligence and high volumes of text-based content), the NCECC and police services may not have the necessary resources to investigate all incidents that are identified, and may also face significant challenges once investigations are begun. The data likely reflect the number of active or closed investigations for each year rather than the total number of incidents reported to police, accounting for only a subset of suspected CSAEM incidents within Canada.

Prior to 2020, the number of cybercrimes is an undercount as some police services were unable to report the cybercrime indicator for all years. The data exclude the Quebec City Police in 2014 and 2015, the municipal police service of Calgary from 2014 to 2016, the Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) from 2014 to 2017, both the Saint John Police Force and the Canadian Forces Military Police from 2014 to 2019 and Dryden, a detachment of the OPP in 2022. For 2023 and 2024, the data exclude Saint John Police Force.

Bill C-291 received Royal Assent on October 10, 2024, with amendments to Criminal Code sections 163.1(2–4.1) effective October 10, 2025. In response, the Canadian Centre for Justice and Community Safety Statistics (CCJCSS) adjusted the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey by renaming violation codes 3455 and 3456 to “Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (possessing/accessing; making/distributing)”.

police-quarterly.text: Data coverage for preliminary police-reported data varies monthly. Preliminary data was reported by police services covering between 91% and 99% of the population of Canada. Monthly data may be incomplete due to ongoing police investigations or delays in data entry. Official annual police-reported data are available in July each year. For official published annual statistics on hate crime and cybercrime, see the following online data tables: 35-10-0066, 35-10-0067, 35-10-0191, 35-10-0001, 35-10-0002.

These are preliminary data and are expected to differ from final official annual results released in the summer each year. They reflect all microdata monthly submissions received from police services prior to the date the data were finalized for release. As a result, some months may be incomplete. Once data for a quarter are released, they are not retroactively updated. Therefore, year-to-date data may not equal the total of the most recently released quarter and the previous quarter’s year-to-date total.

Preliminary quarterly data represent incidents reported to police between the start and end of each calendar quarter (Q1 – January 1 to March 31; Q2 – April 1 to June 30; Q3 – July 1 to September 30; Q4 – October 1 to December 31).

Year to date data are cumulative and represent incidents reported to police between the start of the calendar year (January 1st) and the end of each calendar quarter (for example, ‘Q2- Year-to-Date’ includes incidents reported between January 1st and June 30th).

Percentage change values have not been calculated as there may be variations in the number of police services reporting from one period to the next which could result in false comparisons between quarters.
Selected data at the regional level have been suppressed due to small counts and to protect confidentiality.

Counts for making or distribution of child sexual abuse and exploitation material are affected by the number of cases coming to the attention of Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) detachments in British Columbia through a partnership with the British Columbia Integrated Child Exploitation Unit (BC ICE Unit) and the National Child Exploitation Crime Centre (NCECC). The counts may vary from quarter to quarter due to the timing of file sharing between the NCECC, BC ICE Unit and RCMP detachments.

A census metropolitan area (CMA) consists of one or more neighbouring municipalities situated around a major urban core. A CMA must have a total population of at least 100,000, of which 50,000 or more live in the urban core. To be included in the CMA, other adjacent municipalities must have a high degree of integration with the central urban core, as measured by commuting flows derived from census data. A CMA typically comprises more than one police service. CMA populations have been adjusted to follow policing boundaries. The Oshawa CMA is excluded from this analysis owing to the incongruity between the police service jurisdictional boundaries and the CMA boundaries.  Lethbridge, Alberta and Belleville, Ontario became new CMAs as of the 2016 Census. Fredericton, New Brunswick; Drummondville, Quebec; Red Deer, Alberta; Kamloops, British Columbia; Chilliwack, British Columbia and Nanaimo, British Columbia became new CMAs as of the 2021 Census. Coverage for each CMA is virtually 100%, except in Toronto (approx. 90%), and Hamilton (approx. 76%).
Excluded from this table are the small number of police services that do not report to the Uniform Crime Reporting Survey (UCR) 2.

The increase in cybercrime incidents may be a result of the increase in incidents of child pornography between 2014 and 2015, which can be in part attributed to a proactive project initiated by the British Columbia Integrated Child Exploitation Unit which recorded Internet Protocol (IP) addresses that were in possession of, and possibly sharing child pornography. As this initiative focused on Victoria in 2015, notable increases in these offences were reported by this jurisdiction.
Calgary Police Service cybercrime data for 2017 and onward are suspected cybercrimes only and should be interpreted with caution.

Data coverage for police-reported data varies slightly each year. Cybercrime data for 2025 covers 99.6% of the Canadian population. Coverage for each province/territory is virtually 100% with the exception of New Brunswick (90.9%) due to the exclusion of Saint John Police Force. These percentages are based on police-reported data and populations for the 2025 data cycle.

Hate crime, organized crime and cybercrime data from the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey are now revised back one year with each annual release. This approach was introduced for the 2019 data release and was applied to the 2018 revised data.

Annual counts of cybercrime offences for Toronto Police Service increase when revised data are published one year after the initial release. This is due to lengthy investigations required to confirm whether or not the incident is in fact a cybercrime. Therefore, changes between the most recent year of data and the previous year should be interpreted with caution.

Saint John Police Force cybercrime data are unverified for the years they are included (from 2020 to 2022) and therefore represent incidents that are suspected cybercrimes only and should be interpreted with caution.

It is important to note that while official police-reported data on crime from the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey use Statistics Canada's standard Census Metropolitan Area (CMA) names, the boundaries for the policing-based CMAs do not always fully align with the standard CMA geographic units used for disseminating information about the Census of Population.

Under the authority of the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal (CFPM), the Canadian Forces Military Police Group (CF MP Gp) provides professional policing, security, and detention services to the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and the Department of National Defence (DND) globally, across the full spectrum of military operations. Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey data for the CF MP Gp represent only crimes committed in Canada, on or in relation to DND property or assets, investigated by the military police. Within Canada, in many instances, the military police share concurrent jurisdiction with civilian police. In the enforcement of Canadian military and criminal laws, military police are peace officers and lawfully exercise jurisdiction over members of the CAF and over persons on defence establishments including civilians.

Under the authority of the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal (CFPM), the Canadian Forces Military Police Group (CF MP Gp) is now reporting incidents to the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey. They have provided incidents going back to January 2020 and are not included in 2025. Data from the Office of the CFPM are aggregated at the national level to account for small counts and to protect confidentiality. Therefore, provincial and territorial totals will not equal Canada-level totals. Crime Severity Index data and rates are not available.

Prior to 2020, the number of cybercrimes is an undercount as some police services were unable to report the cybercrime indicator for all years. The data exclude the Quebec City Police in 2014 and 2015, the municipal police service of Calgary from 2014 to 2016, the Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) from 2014 to 2017, both the Saint John Police Force and the Canadian Forces Military Police from 2014 to 2019 and Dryden, a detachment of the OPP in 2022. For 2023, the data exclude Saint John Police Force.
The census metropolitan area (CMA) of Belleville-Quinte West was formerly known as Belleville.

The marked increase in 2023 for London is mostly attributed to the start of online reporting for fraud violations by London Police Service (LPS), which resulted in an influx of reports being generated. In addition, efforts have been made by LPS to improve their reporting of financial crime and cyber-enabled crimes that have a computer as the target of the offence. Comparisons to previous years should be made with caution.
